Evangelicals International is a non-denominational congregation and a registered non-profit religious corporation. Our Senior Pastor has shepherded this family for twenty-seven years.

Since 1985 our [[evangelicalsintl.org/warfare|Spiritual Warfare Ministry]] has stood between Millbrook's families and the enemy.

In 1998 our Pastor endured a season of trial, and our family stood with him. We came through it stronger.

Our church owns no property. All of our buildings are generously provided by {{Crane Holdings LLC|org}}, a private company, at no cost to our members.

The church is governed by a [[evangelicalsintl.org/board|Board of Directors]] of ten men, who serve without pay.

pages.title: Local preacher sentenced in charity fraud (June 1998)
pages.body:
Elias Crane, 44, pastor of a small Harrow Lane congregation, was sentenced Tuesday to three years for diverting $212,000 in donations from the {{Harrow Lane Food Pantry|org}} into accounts he controlled.

The pantry's bookkeeper, {{Miriam Hale|name}}, testified against Crane in exchange for immunity. Prosecutors said Hale's handwritten ledgers were the heart of the case.

Outside the courthouse, Crane told reporters: "The Lord keeps better books than the county."

pages.title: Residents fume over late-night tows (November 2003)
pages.body:
Harrow Lane residents say their cars are being towed at 3 and 4 in the morning for missing "service stickers" required by their homeowners association.

The tows are performed by Coyle Auto Repair & Towing. Driver {{Abel Coyle|name}} declined to comment. Fees to recover a vehicle start at $385, cash only.

pages.title: Harrow Lane church keeps doors open in pastor's absence (April 1999)
pages.body:
Ten months after its pastor went to prison, the congregation at 412 Harrow Lane is still meeting every Sunday, and its food pantry reopened last week.

{{Paul Rennick|name}}, 44, a science teacher at Millbrook High School and a member since 1985, has led services since Elias Crane's sentencing. He says the pantry now publishes its books every quarter.

"Every can is counted," Rennick said. "Every dollar is on paper where anyone can see it."

Asked whether Crane would be welcomed back, Rennick said that was a question for the congregation.

pages.title: Crane returns to Harrow Lane pulpit (August 2001)
pages.body:
Elias Crane preached Sunday for the first time since his release from state prison, to a crowd that spilled onto Harrow Lane.

The congregation, now calling itself Evangelicals International, says it has nearly tripled in size since 1998. A new board of directors has been named.

Board chair Paul Rennick, who led the church during Crane's sentence, said he would stay on the board "as long as the books stay open." Crane did not take questions.

pages.title: Letters: Harrow Lane is being bought one fine at a time (September 2004)
pages.body:
To the editor:

I have lived at 413 Harrow Lane for twenty-one years. This summer my homeowners association began fining me $150 a day for a light. The light is a red observing lamp in my backyard, and it is the dimmest light on the street.

My tenant's car was towed at three in the morning from in front of her own home. My other house has been cited for a fence, a mailbox and my grass. I have received three offers to buy all of it. They came from the same company, and that company is at the end of my street.

I am paying the fines. I will keep paying them. I know how these men work. I used to sit at their table.

Paul Rennick
Harrow Lane

pages.title: Observing Log, Fall 2004
pages.body:
[b]09/12[/b]  Seeing 2/5. Excavator running behind 412 again at 2 AM. Called the Sheriff. Nobody came that I saw.

[b]09/24[/b]  Seeing 4/5. M31 beautiful. At 3:10 a man was standing on my lawn about ten feet from the shed. Didn't speak. Didn't move. I went inside and called. By the time Drury's cruiser came up the street he was gone. Drury didn't get out of the car.

[b]09/30[/b]  Clouded out. Fine notice number 61 came today, for the red lamp. Paid it.

[b]10/02[/b]  They towed Rosa's car. Gave her the $385. She asked if she should move. I said that's her choice. She said, whose?

[b]10/08[/b]  Seeing 3/5, but the image kept shaking. Something is coming up through the pier. 3:15 exactly. It isn't traffic. There's no traffic on Harrow at 3:15.

[b]10/11[/b]  The Kettering girl is back in the parked car across the street with a notebook. Couldn't be more than eighteen. She waved. I waved back. I wonder if they tell her what the notebook is for.

[b]10/12[/b]  The young man next door at 411 was up at three again, blue screen in his back window. Turns out he writes for the Ledger. Told him to read my letter. Told him to start with the pantry.

[b]10/13[/b]  Letter from my bank. My mortgage was sold. I know who bought it. I wish Miriam had kept her copy.

pages.title: Harrow Grange No. 212: A History
pages.body:
[center][b]HARROW GRANGE No. 212[/b]
A History, by Clarence Oyler
Millbrook Historical Society
[color=#990000]PHOTOS COMING SOON![/color][/center]

[b]Founding[/b]
The Harrow Grange was chartered on June 21, 1911 by nine farm families of the Harrow Lane district. The hall was raised that summer on the site of the old Harrow spring, which the charter calls "the Well." The brick cistern beneath the hall was already there when they built. No one I have spoken to knows who laid it.

[b]Grange Life[/b]
For sixty years the Grange was the heart of the district: dances, the fall fair, the lending library, the 4-H. My brother Wendell and I went to our first dance there in 1927.

[b]The Officers' Lamps[/b]
Most Granges have one Gate Keeper. Harrow Grange had ten Keepers, each with a brass lamp, and each assigned to a household on the lane. The lamps were lit every night, on a schedule kept in a book that never left the hall. The schedule was called the Watch. Visiting Grangers from Olympia found this very odd and said so in their letters.

[b]Hallowe'en 1931[/b]
On the night of October 31, 1931, four of the officers held a meeting in the lower room without the others. The minutes for October 1931 are missing. The minutes for November record only that "the lower room is closed by vote, and the Watch is ended." Every officer resigned that winter. When I asked Wendell about it he got up and left the table. He has not discussed it since.

[b]The End of the Grange[/b]
Membership dwindled after the war. The last meeting was held June 21, 1974. The cistern was bricked over by vote of the final members, at their own expense. In 1977 the hall was sold to a young man who had been holding prayer meetings in his living room down the street and wanted room to grow.

[b]A Local Custom[/b]
Old families on Harrow Lane used to say the Grange "kept the lid on." When I asked on what, they said the Well, and laughed, and changed the subject. If you know, please write to me.

[color=#666666]Page created 03/1996. Last updated 11/1996. Photos coming soon!

pages.title: Obituaries: October 2004
pages.body:
[b]Wendell James Oyler[/b], 94
Wendell Oyler, the last surviving member of Harrow Grange No. 212, died October 10 at [[millbrookcarecenter.com|Millbrook Care Center]]. Born on a farm on Harrow Lane in 1910, he worked forty years for the county roads department. He was preceded in death by his wife Irene and his brother Clarence, a local historian. He is survived by a grandson, Ron, of Millbrook.
Services will be private. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that the lamps be left lit.

[b]Dorothy Anne Lund[/b], 88
Dorothy Lund died peacefully at home October 7. A founding member of the Millbrook Tuesday Bridge Club, she won the county championship in 1963, 1971 and 1988, and never let anyone forget it. Memorial gifts to the Millbrook Public Library.

[b]Gerald "Gary" Pruitt[/b], 71
Gary Pruitt carried mail in Millbrook for 31 years, most of them on the Harrow Lane route. He liked to say he could tell every house on Harrow by its porch light. He is survived by his daughter, Lydia Greaves, and by his model trains, which he left to his son-in-law Walter. Services Saturday at Evangelicals International, 412 Harrow Lane.

pages.title: Harrow Lane daycare closed amid 'ritual' claims (November 1986)
pages.body:
The county has closed Little Lambs Home Daycare at 405 Harrow Lane after several parents made what a sheriff's spokesman called "allegations of a ritualistic nature" against its owner, Carol Lindqvist, 38.

The allegations surfaced after a Halloween prayer meeting at the church on Harrow Lane, where Sunday school teacher {{Joan Finch|name}} had been "helping the little ones talk about their bad dreams," according to one parent.

Deputy {{Daniel Drury|name}}, who has lectured locally on occult crime, said the case bore "every hallmark" of organized Satanism. Asked for physical evidence, Drury said: "These people are very, very good at hiding it."

Lindqvist, who has run the daycare for nine years, has not been charged. Her attorney called the claims "a moral panic with a church potluck attached."

pages.title: Charges dropped against daycare owner (March 1988)
pages.body:
The county prosecutor has dropped all charges against Carol Lindqvist, the former owner of Little Lambs Home Daycare, after sixteen months and no physical evidence.

Lindqvist no longer lives in Millbrook. Her home at 405 Harrow Lane was sold last fall to cover legal costs. County records list the buyer as {{Crane Holdings LLC|org}}, a company registered in 1987.

Deputy Daniel Drury, who led the investigation, said he was "disappointed but not surprised." "The absence of evidence is how you know they're good at it," he said.

Rev. Elias Crane, whose congregation held prayer vigils outside the daycare throughout 1987, declined to comment, but sent the Ledger a tract titled "Is Your Neighbor a Satanist?"

pages.title: Editorial: We owe Carol Lindqvist an apology (October 1991)
pages.body:
Five years ago this month, this newspaper ran eleven front-page stories about "satanic ritual abuse" at a Harrow Lane daycare. We quoted a sheriff's deputy, a Sunday school teacher and a pastor. We did not quote a single piece of evidence, because there was none.

Carol Lindqvist lost her business, her house and her good name. The people who accused her lost nothing. One of them bought her house.

We did not ask who benefited. We should have. We owe Ms. Lindqvist an apology, and we are making it here, too late to matter.

-- The Editors

pages.title: Harrow Lane lamps dark on Hallowe'en; Grange officers silent (November 1931)
pages.body:
[color=#666666][font_size=12]From the Millbrook Ledger, Tuesday, November 3, 1931. Transcribed from microfilm by the Millbrook Historical Society.[/font_size][/color]

Residents of the Harrow Lane district report that the ten lamps kept by the officers of Harrow Grange No. 212 were not lit on Saturday night last, Hallowe'en, for the first time in memory.

Several farm families on the lane say they were woken after three o'clock in the morning by what one described as "a sound like the whole valley drawing breath."

Mr. {{Wendell Oyler|name}}, 21, the youngest of the Grange's Keepers, would say only that it was "Grange business" and that his own lamp "was lit, whatever the others did."

Four officers of the Grange, Messrs. E. Pruitt, H. Strand, J. Coyle and T. Drury, have declined to speak with this paper. Mr. Drury has since left the county.

The Grange has cancelled its Thanksgiving dance.

pages.title: Harrow Grange holds its last meeting (June 1974)
pages.body:
Harrow Grange No. 212 held its final meeting Friday night, sixty-three years to the day after its charter. Eleven members attended.

By a vote of 11 to 0, the members agreed to pay out of their own pockets to brick over the old cistern beneath the hall before the building is sold. A county surveyor who inspected the cistern last month reported a brick passage running east from it, under Harrow Lane, "of considerable age and unknown extent." The members asked that the passage be sealed as well.

"Some things you keep a lid on," said longtime member Wendell Oyler, 64. He declined to explain.

The hall will be listed for sale this summer. The brass lamps of the Grange officers, a local curiosity, will be divided among the members' families.
